12.1.crux: Friction is a force between two surfaces in contact that opposes their motion against each other.

cards.title: Friction opposes motion
say: When you push a book across a table, it slows down and stops.
A force between the book and the table acts against the motion: friction.
cards.remember: Friction acts in the direction opposite to motion.

cards.title: Everyday friction

items.text: Bicycle slows when you stop pedalling

say: Friction is all around us, though we rarely notice it.

cards.title: Both surfaces

cols.head: Upper surface
cells: Feels friction from the lower surface

cols.head: Lower surface
cells: Feels friction from the upper surface

say: Friction acts on both surfaces that are in contact.

crux_points: Friction acts between two surfaces in contact.
It opposes the relative motion between them.

quiz.q: A book pushed along a table stops because of…
quiz.why: Friction between the book and table opposes its motion.

quiz.q: In which direction does friction act?
quiz.why: Friction always opposes the motion between surfaces.

12.2.crux: Friction comes from tiny bumps on surfaces locking into each other; rougher surfaces and harder pressing give more friction, and it's harder to start something moving than to keep it sliding.

cards.title: Zoom in on a surface
say: Under a magnifier, all surfaces have tiny hills and valleys.
These irregularities interlock, and we need force to get them past each other.

cards.title: What changes friction
say: Rough surfaces have bigger bumps, so more interlocking.
A heavier object presses the surfaces together harder, so friction increases.

cards.title: Starting vs sliding

cols.head: Static friction
cells: To start moving an object at rest

cols.head: Sliding friction
cells: When the object is already sliding

say: It is harder to start pushing a heavy box than to keep it moving.
Once it slides, the bumps don't get time to lock in as deeply.

crux_points: Friction comes from interlocking irregularities on surfaces.
Rougher surfaces and stronger pressing give more friction.
Static friction (to start) is bigger than sliding friction.

quiz.q: Why does a rough surface have more friction?
quiz.why: Bigger irregularities lock together more strongly.
It takes more force to start an object moving than to keep it sliding.

12.3.crux: Friction is a 'necessary evil': we couldn't walk, write or brake without it, but it also wears things out and wastes energy as heat.

cards.title: We need friction
say: On a wet, slippery floor we can hardly walk, because there's too little friction.

cards.title: But friction also harms
say: Rubbing slowly wears away surfaces: this is wear and tear.

cards.title: Friction makes heat

steps.text: They get warm: friction produces heat
In machines this heat is wasted energy

say: That's why friction is called a necessary evil.
cards.remember: Necessary: grip and control. Evil: wear and wasted heat.

crux_points: Friction lets us walk, hold, write and brake.
It wears out shoes, tyres and machine parts.
It produces heat, wasting energy in machines.

quiz.q: Why is it hard to walk on a wet marble floor?
quiz.why: Water makes the floor slippery, reducing the friction we need to grip.

quiz.q: Your hands get warm when you rub them. This shows friction…

12.4.crux: We increase friction with grooves and rough grips, and reduce it with lubricants like oil and grease, powder, and wheels.

cards.title: When we want MORE friction
say: Grooves and rough materials increase friction where we need grip.

cards.title: When we want LESS friction
say: Substances that reduce friction are called lubricants.
Oil forms a thin layer between surfaces so they don't rub directly.
cards.remember: Lubricant = a substance that reduces friction.

cards.title: How a lubricant works
say: With oil between them, the surfaces barely touch.
In some machines, a cushion of air between parts reduces friction even more.

crux_points: Grooves, treads and rough grips increase friction.
Lubricants (oil, grease, graphite) and powder reduce friction.
A thin layer between surfaces keeps their bumps from interlocking.

options: To increase friction with the road
quiz.why: Treads give a better grip on the road.

quiz.q: Oil put between moving machine parts is a…
quiz.why: Lubricants reduce friction between moving parts.

12.5.crux: Rolling is much easier than sliding: rolling friction is smaller, so we use wheels and ball bearings.

cards.title: Slide or roll?

cols.head: Sliding
cells: Drag a heavy box on the floor

say: When one object rolls over another, the friction is called rolling friction.
It is smaller than sliding friction.

cards.title: Ball bearings
say: Ball bearings replace sliding with rolling.
They are used in ceiling fans, bicycles and many machines.

cards.title: The wheel changed the world
say: Because rolling friction is small, wheels let us move heavy loads easily.

crux_points: Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction.
Wheels make moving heavy loads easy.
Ball bearings reduce friction in fans, bicycles and machines.

quiz.q: Which part is marked '?' in the ball bearing?
quiz.why: The steel balls roll between the rings, replacing sliding with rolling.

options: Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction
quiz.why: Rolling needs much less force than dragging.

12.6.crux: Air and water also exert friction (drag) on things moving through them; streamlined shapes, like a fish or a plane, reduce it.

cards.title: Friction in fluids
say: Liquids and gases are together called fluids.
Fluids exert a friction force on objects moving through them, called drag.

cards.title: What affects drag
say: Moving objects must use energy to overcome drag.

cards.title: Learning from nature
say: Fish and birds have streamlined bodies: pointed at the front, slim and smooth.
Engineers copy these shapes for boats and aeroplanes.

crux_points: Fluids (liquids and gases) exert friction called drag.
Drag depends on speed, shape and the kind of fluid.
Streamlined shapes like fish, birds and planes reduce drag.

quiz.q: Why are aeroplanes shaped like birds?
quiz.why: A streamlined shape reduces air friction.

quiz.q: The friction exerted by fluids is called…
quiz.why: Fluid friction is also called drag.
